paragraphs.text: FORM No. HCJD/C-121 ORDER SHEET IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT Razia Begum Vs. Awais Tanveer Jathol, etc. Sr. No. of order/ proceedings Date of order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of Parties’ counsel, where necessary 04.11.2026. Nemo for the petitioner. Respondent No.1 ex-parte vide order dated 26.01.2023. Mr. Qamar Hanif Ramay, Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan. M/s Qamar Zaman Qureshi and Barrister Hassan Khalid Ranjha, Additional Advocate Generals Punjab. Mr. Muhammad Abid, Civil Judge/Research Officer, Lahore High Court, Lahore. M/s. Kashif Hussain, Shehryar Farhan Beg, Muhammad Dilbar Ghauri, Subhan Ali, Mazhar Hussain Tahir, Malik Khalid Tanveer, Abdul Manan Sipra, Rana Athar Raza Khan, Fayyaz Sandhu, Barrister Muhammad Sohail Babar Khan, Barrister Saeed Hussain Nagra, Sh. Muhammad Naseer, Barrister Rana Khizar Hayat, Barrister Karim Ullah Sraw, Muhammad Waleed Waheed Chaudhry, Asif Raza Rasheed, Barrister Shahid Masood Khan, Syed Imran Ehsan, Muhammad Ali Butt, Zohaib Hassan Joya. Abdullah Haroon, Muhammad Saeed Bin Noman, Dr. Muhammad Azeem Raja, Syed Ali Allow-u-Din, Umair Yasin Khan, Muhammad Afzal, Mateen ul Haq Ch., M. Haris Jutt, Shafique Ahmad Bhutta, Zahid Saeed, Omer Riaz Chaudhary, Adeel Hassan, Kamran Ahmad, Hafiz Naeem ur Rehman, Barrister Hassan Safdar Khan, Arslan Aamir Tarar, Syed Muhammad Haider Kazmi, Syed Muhammad Nazim Abbas, Haider Zaman Khan, Saeed A. Sheikh, Jehangir Hassan Dogar, Ghulam Murtaza Chaudhry, Zeeshan Ahmad Ali Ranjha, Asad Hayat Bhoon, Sardar Farrukh Mushtaq, Ashiq Ali Rana, Ms. Asifa Ahmad, Ms. Humera Bashir, Ms. Isra Irshad Ms. Musarrat Rehman, Ms. Maryam Khan Khosa, Ms. Zubera Bashir Chaudhry, and Ms. Moniba Nadeem, Advocates. MUZAMIL AKHTAR SHABIR J:- In the present case, the petitioner, Razia Begum (‘petitioner’), who was the defendant in the suit for specific performance with permanent injunctions filed by Respondent No.1, Awais Tanveer Jathol (‘Respondent’) against her has called in question order dated 28.01.2022 passed by learned Civil Judge, Ferozewala and Judgment dated 05.09.2022 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Ferozewala respectively, whereby application for interim relief filed by the respondent had been allowed and appeal filed by the petitioner to challenge the same had been dismissed.

Although no one has appeared on behalf of the petitioner today, yet the perusal of the file shows that on 18.10.2022 the learned counsel for the petitioner had argued that the petitioner was an old lady and respondent, who is her grandson, had obtained stay order against her by filing a suit for specific performance of agreement to sell, which she had never executed, therefore, the impugned orders were not justified. Notice was ordered to be issued for service of respondent, who despite service of notices for 16.12.2022 and 26.01.2023 did not appear and this Court vide order dated 26.01.2023 proceeded ex-parte against him. Thereafter, till today no attempt has been made on his behalf to join the proceedings of the petition by filing an application for setting aside ex-parte proceedings. As this is an old case and parties have not appeared today, hence, the same is being decided in their absence.

The brief background of the case is that the respondent filed a suit for specific performance of agreement to sell against the petitioner in respect of 18 marla land, details of which are mentioned in the plaint by claiming that through agreement to sell dated 04.11.2020 the petitioner has agreed to sell her aforementioned property to him for a consideration of Rs.40,00,000/- which she has received from him in cash while executing the agreement to sell, alongwith the said suit he also filed an application for grant of interim relief to restrain the petitioner from transferring the property any further during the pendency of the suit. The suit and application for interim relief were contested by the petitioner by claiming that she is an old illiterate lady, who has weak eyesight and denied the execution of agreement to sell and having received the sale consideration and claimed that in fact, fraud was committed by the respondent with her as he is her grandson and had obtained her thumb impression on some papers on the pretext of getting financial assistance under the Benazir Income Support Scheme and further submitted that she had built shops upon the suit land by spending Rs.12,00,000/-, which were forcibly demolished by the respondent and in this regard, a criminal case bearing FIR No.253 of 21 was registered under Sections 447, 427, 511, 148 and 149 PPC with Police Station Narang, Sheikhupura against the respondent and on the basis of said grounds she pleaded for dismissal of the suit as well as application for interim relief. The application for interim relief was allowed by the trial court and appeal filed by the petitioner thereagainst was dismissed. Both the aforesaid order and judgment are under challenge before this Court through the instant revision petition.

The question for consideration before this Court is whether both the courts were justified to grant interim relief in favour of the respondent as the petitioner despite admitting her thumb impression, had categorically denied the execution of agreement to sell in favour of the respondent. To determine the said aspect of the matter, it would be important to refer to the order and judgment passed by both the courts below.

The learned trial court, while granting interim relief vide order dated 28.01.2022, had observed as under:- ‘From the perusal of the record, it reveals that plaintiff in plaint alleged that defendant was owner of the suit property who entered into an agreement to sell regarding the suit property with him in consideration of Rs. 40,00,000/-, received all consideration amount and possession of the suit property was handed over to him and defendant in her written statement did not deny her thumb impressions on the alleged agreement to sell. Contention of the defendant that on pretext of drawing amount from Benazir Income Support plaintiff fraudulently obtained her thumb impression on different papers can only be determined after recording of evidence. So, in presence of written agreement to sell regarding the suit property in favour of the plaintiff, plaintiff established a prima-facie case in his favour, balance of inconvenience also lies in favour of the plaintiff and if the defendant will interfere into alleged possession of the plaintiff over the suit property and further alienation of the suit property then it will be the plaintiff who will suffer irreparable loss. So, in view of above discussion instant application is hereby accepted as prayed for.’

The appellate court dismissed the petitioner’s appeal against the said order and maintained the order of trial court, whereby interim relief had been granted while observing as under:- ‘Perusal of the record shows that although agreement to sell is denied by appellant but she admitted her thumb impression on the agreement to sell alleging that same was result of fraud committed by appellant. It is settled principle of law that a party would be bound to prove a fact which he/she alleges. The burden of proving fraud in obtaining her thumb impression on the agreement to sell dated 04.10.2020 is also on the shoulder of appellant. It is settled law that if a case requires detail analysis of evidence, it does not have a prima facie case. The case of present appellant requires analysis of evidence regarding the allegation of fraud, so she has no prima facie case in her favour. The suit property is in the shape of dismantled shops over which both the parties claimed their possession but there is no proof with any party. So, it is better to preserve the suit property till the decision of suit and it is the respondent who shall suffer irreparable loss if the suit property is further alienated during the pendency of the suit especially when he has allegedly paid all the consideration amount. Therefore, the impugned order was rightly passed by learned trial court in accordance with law governing the grant or refusal of injunction. Hence, the findings of learned trial court are upheld with the result that appeal has no force and the same is dismissed. The copy of the order be sent to learned trial court and record of learned trial be returned immediately.’

Both the courts while allowing the application for interim relief filed by the respondent have given undue weightage to the fact that petitioner had admitted her thumb impression on the alleged agreement to sell, whereas the salient features of the case have been ignored inasmuch as it was ignored that she had claimed that she was an old illiterate lady and fraud was committed by the respondent, her grandson, who obtained her thumb impression on some papers for purpose of getting financial assistance for her under the Benazir Income Support Scheme, which means that she had disowned the very purpose for which the thumb impression had been obtained and also challenged the nature of transaction for which the document (i.e. agreement to sell) subject matter of the suit had been executed, hence the maxim of non est factum would be applicable to the instant case. Reliance in this regard is placed on Mst. Waris Jan and another versus Liaqat Ali and others (PLD 2019 Lahore 333), wherein it is provided as under:- “The maxim "non est factum" (Latin for "it is not my deed", which is a defence in contract law that allows signing party to escape performance of an agreement which is fundamentally different from what he or she intended to execute or sign) was thus found imbedded in the defence of the first defendant. It is contended on behalf of the plaintiff that it is settled principle of law that in a suit for specific performance where the defendant admits his/her thumb impression on the sale agreement but alleges that his/her thumb impression was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation on blank papers which have been converted into sale agreement subsequently, the burden to prove the same lies on the defendant; and, that since in the instant case the first defendant did not appear in the witness box to state her own case on oath and did not offer herself to be cross- examined by the plaintiff, a presumption would arise that the case set up by her was not correct. The said argument is neither well founded nor sufficient to prove the validity of the agreement to sell dated 19th July, 2007 (Ex.P-1). Ordinarily, the person who challenges the validity of a transaction on the ground of fraud, undue influence, etc. and charges his opponent with bad faith has to discharge the burden of proof which rests on him. But the major exception to this rule is that the initial burden would not shift to the party who challenges the transaction and will instead be cast on the person who relies on such deed or document if it is brought to the notice of the Courts that grantor is illiterate. Even otherwise in the case on hands the suit was for specific performance, and, therefore, it was for the plaintiff to prove his case, and agreement for sale (Ex.P-1) and non-examination of the first defendant in the Court was of no consequence, especially when she was not called upon to prove any other aspect but her defence only by cross-examining the plaintiff's witnesses and, therefore, no adverse inference could be drawn against the first defendant because she did not enter the witness-box.’

Time and again the Superior Courts of this country have held that special care and caution has to be taken and compliance of safeguards articulated in judgments of superior courts has mandatorily to be made in cases of purda nashin ladies, wherein it is alleged that they had either transferred their property or agreed to transfer property owned by them to another party, whereas the said transaction had been disputed by or on behalf of such ladies. Reliance is placed on Muhammad Ishfaq and another versus Salma Begum (2026 SCMR 1523), wherein it is held that in cases involving parda nashin or similarly placed women, the Supreme Court has consistently exercised heightened caution and has emphasized compliance with the safeguards articulated in the cases of Phul Peer Shah versus Hafeez Fatima (2016 SCMR 1225), Ghulam Farid and another versus Sher Rehman through LRs (2016 SCMR 862) and Ghulam Muhammad versus Zohran Bibi and others (2021 SCMR 19), which largely include that the party relying upon such a transaction must prove that it was entered into with the woman’s free will and informed consent, that its nature and consequences were explained to her in a language she understood, that she had the benefit of independent and disinterested advice, that the witnesses were trustworthy and free from any conflict of interest and that the sale consideration was duly paid and received by her.

Moreover, both the courts while reaching said conclusion instead of observing that the burden to prove the agreement to sell was upon the respondent/plaintiff, as the execution of same had been denied by the petitioner, observed that the burden was upon the petitioner who was the defendant of the suit to prove that the agreement had been executed by fraud, which was not justified for the reason that burden of proof is always on the beneficiary of the documents to prove its genuineness and the plaintiff has to stand on his own legs instead of relying upon the weaknesses of the other party. Reliance is placed on Abdul Majeed and others versus Mst. Khalida Bibi (deceased) through L.Rs. and others (2026 SCMR 587), Sultan versus Noor Asghar (2020 SCMR 682), Anwar Sajid versus Abdul Rashid Khan and another (2011 SCMR 958) and Sultan Muhammad and another versus Muhammad Qasim and others (2010 SCMR 1630), wherein it is mentioned that any party approaching court for grant of relief would have to discharge his own burden and stand on his own legs to succeed and could not avail benefit of any weakness in case of opposite party. In view of the principles laid down in the said judgments, unless the respondent as plaintiff has discharged the burden of establishing the genuineness of agreement to sell and payment of consideration through cogent evidence, the burden to prove the execution of agreement through fraud could not shift upon the petitioner/defendant as asking the petitioner to prove that agreement had been executed with fraud before its execution was established by the respondent through evidence would amount to putting the cart before the horse, which was not permissible under the law. Reliance is placed on Mazhar Saeed and another versus A.D.J. and 11 others (2011 YLR 3089 Lahore), wherein it has been laid down that where a specific plea or fact is asserted by a party in pleadings, such party would be bound to prove positively such plea or fact by producing convincing and cogent evidence, whereafter opposite party could be required to disprove the same and the opposite party could never be directed to prove negative fact before positive fact is proved as same would amount to putting horse before cart. Somewhat similar principles have been laid down in Khursheed Begum and others versus Inam-ur- Rehman Khan and others (PLD 2009 Lahore 552).

In the case in hand, the courts below while granting interim relief did not take into consideration any of the aforementioned safeguards and merely by observing that thumb impression had not been denied by the petitioner and sale consideration had allegedly been paid by the respondent, granted interim relief to him, which was not based on proper exercise of jurisdiction vested in the said courts. The glaring omission was that it was not considered by both courts whether any independent advice was available to the petitioner and whether the said agreement had been entered into between the parties with free will of the petitioner, who had consistently been denying the proper execution of the said agreement. She denied having received any sale consideration but the appellate court categorically mentioned that the respondent had allegedly paid the sale consideration amount, which means that the said court itself was not sure that whether said amount had been paid or not, yet relied upon the same for granting relief to the respondent. The said court could at least have asked the respondent to show through which means he had made payment of sale consideration of Rs.40,00,000/- and how he had arranged such a huge amount and handed over the same to the petitioner in cash and what source was available with her for safe keeping of such huge amount, especially when independent advice was not shown to be available with her for the said transaction. Merely by mentioning that said transaction was made in the presence of witnesses would not grant sanctity to the said transaction unless the witnesses enter the witness box and proved the said transaction through cogent evidence. It is important to note here that the burden to prove payment of sale consideration is always on the beneficiary of the document. Reliance is placed on Muhammad Zubair and 4 others versus Mst. Zamrood Jan (2025 YLR 2779 Lahore), whereas in the present case the courts by mentioning that respondent has allegedly paid entire sale consideration impliedly shifted the burden upon the petitioner to prove that the said consideration had not been paid, which was not justified by any stretch of imagination.

Furthermore, while granting interim relief both the courts below have not properly appreciated the fact that petitioner was an old illiterate lady who claimed that respondent had obtained her thumb impression for the purpose of obtaining a financial relief under Benazir Income Support Scheme and she was acting under his influence, hence the factum of undue influence could not be ruled out. It is pertinent to mention here that use of undue influence to deprive a woman of her property would vitiate such a transaction. Reliance may be placed on principles laid down in the judgment reported as Abrar Hussain versus Mst. Bibi Shahida and others (PLD 2026 SC 42), wherein it has been held that those who, through coercion, deceit, or undue influence deprive women of this divinely bestowed right must be held accountable under the law and made answerable. A society, that turns a blind eye to deprivation of inheritance rights to its women defies the spirit of Constitution and express Command of Almighty Allah. The strength of a nation lies in the protection of its most vulnerable classes. A State that fails to safeguard the inheritance rights to its women fails in its duty to uphold the principles of equity, faith and justice.

In the case in hand it is also disputed that who holds the possession of property and under what right. Needless to mention that merely being in possession of the suit property does not entitle the respondent for interim relief for holding the property for indefinite time span in his suit for specific performance of agreement to sell unless, he had established the execution of said agreement to sell and the fact of the petitioner having received payment of consideration and delivery of possession under the same, which had not been done, hence, there was no prima facie case in favour of the respondent for grant of interim relief by restraining the petitioner from further alienating the suit property during the pendency of the suit. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Muhammad Ali v. Mahnga Khan (2004 SCMR 1111), Muhammad Ahmad Farooq and another v. Province of Punjab through Member Judicial-VII, BOR, Punjab Lahore through DCO/Collector District Sahiwal and 12 others (2018 MLD 959) and Muhammad Ajmal Khan v. Mst. Iqbal Mai (PLJ 2018 Lahore 907). In view of the foregoing, it should have been assumed that there was no prima facie case in favour of the respondent/plaintiff, instead of assuming that the petitioner/defendant lacked any prima facie case in her favour, which was a strange reasoning that prevailed with the courts below to pass order against the petitioner and in favour of the respondent and in the given circumstances of the case may even be termed as perverse.

In addition to above, the learned appellate court on the basis of alleged payment of consideration by the respondent, which had not been established on the record, wrongly concluded that the balance of convenience was in favour of the respondent, whereas the petitioner was likely to suffer more in case interim relief was granted as her possession had been disturbed by the respondent without establishing payment of consideration, hence, balance of convenience was in favour of the petitioner instead of the respondent and there was no valid or justifiable reason for both the subordinate courts to observe that the respondent would suffer an irreparable loss in case interim relief was not granted. Consequently, ingredients for grant of interim relief in favour of the respondent were not made out.

Moreover, it has also not been considered that why the petitioner, who is an old lady and dependent upon the respondent for her affairs as claimed by her, would back out of the agreement after receiving payment of consideration against the same as alleged by the respondent and also get the aforementioned FIR registered against him.

In view of what has been discussed above, it is held that both the courts below had not properly exercised the jurisdiction vested in them by placing the burden upon the petitioner to prove the negative side of the issue without requiring the petitioner to prove positive side of issue by leading cogent evidence to prove the valid execution of agreement to sell and payment in terms of the same to receive possession under the said agreement. Consequently, order and judgment passed by both the courts below are not sustainable and are set aside, by observing that the interim relief granted in favour of the respondent was unjustified and not warranted under the law.
In view of the foregoing, this petition is allowed in the afore-referred terms. (MUZAMIL AKHTAR SHABIR) JUDGE Naveed* APPROVED FOR REPORTING:
